nameStory: The 'creeping' in creeping bellflower comes from its sneaky underground roots that spread and pop up new plants far from where you first spotted them. The 'bellflower' part is obvious once you see those distinctive purple-blue blooms that look just like tiny church bells hanging from the stem. This plant truly lives up to its name by creeping through gardens and wild spaces alike!
description: Creeping bellflower is a tall perennial plant that can reach 2-4 feet high, with a sturdy upright stem topped by a spike of beautiful purple-blue bell-shaped flowers. Originally from Europe and Asia, this plant has made itself very much at home in New England, sometimes a little too much so! The flowers hang like little lanterns along one side of the stem, while the leaves are heart-shaped to oval with toothed edges. Though pretty, it's considered invasive in many areas because of its aggressive spreading habit.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple-blue bell-shaped flowers about 1 inch long hang downward from one side of the stem in a long spike, like tiny church bells on a rope - you can almost imagine them ringing in a breeze

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to oval leaves with sharply toothed edges feel slightly rough and papery to the touch, arranged alternately up the stem with the largest leaves at the bottom

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall single stems rise 2-4 feet high from spreading underground roots, often appearing in patches or colonies rather than single plants

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small dry capsules develop where flowers were, splitting open to release tiny seeds - shake a dried stem and you'll hear them rattle inside

habitat: You'll find creeping bellflower in disturbed soils, roadsides, old fields, woodland edges, and unfortunately for many gardeners, flower beds and lawns. It thrives in both sunny and partially shaded spots and isn't picky about soil type. Often seen growing alongside other weedy species in areas that have been disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground roots, with fresh heart-shaped leaves appearing first. Young plants form low rosettes before sending up flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, with those characteristic purple-blue bells opening from bottom to top along the flower spike. This is when the plant is most easily identified.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature, turning brown and papery. Seeds disperse in late fall, and the above-ground parts begin to die back.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground stems die back completely, but those persistent underground roots remain very much alive, ready to send up new shoots in spring.

funFact: This innocent-looking wildflower is actually a master escape artist - it can grow new plants from tiny pieces of root left behind when you try to dig it up, meaning that attempting to remove it can actually help it spread even faster!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bellflowers, but creeping bellflower's flowers hang distinctly to one side of the stem rather than being evenly arranged all around. Remember: 'creeping bellflower leans to one side' - just like it's trying to sneak away from you!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its pretty flowers, creeping bellflower is considered an invasive species in much of North America and is actually banned from sale in some states. Many gardeners have a love-hate relationship with this plant - they appreciate its beauty but struggle with its aggressive spreading nature.
compareHints: Unlike the delicate common harebell with its slender nodding flowers, creeping bellflower is much taller and more robust with larger, more substantial bell-shaped blooms. The clustered bellflower has flowers bunched together in tight groups rather than strung along one side of the stem. Giant bellflower is even taller but has much larger leaves and flowers that face more outward rather than hanging downward.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Intermediate bellflower sits between common harebell (which is smaller and more delicate) and the larger, showier bellflowers like giant bellflower.

Unlike the more common creeping bellflower which has rougher, heart-shaped leaves and smaller purple flowers, peach-leaved bellflower has distinctively glossy, narrow leaves and much larger cup-shaped blooms.
Unlike the small, delicate bells of common harebell or the upright flower clusters of creeping bellflower, spotted bellflower has distinctly large, pendant flowers with internal spotting.

Unlike its bellflower relatives, clustered bellflower has flowers packed into tight, dense clusters rather than scattered along the stem like creeping bellflower or dangling singly like common harebell.
Among New England's bellflowers, Nettle-leaved Bellflower is distinguished by its robust size and those distinctively serrated, nettle-like leaves.
Unlike its relative the common harebell which grows tall and loose in meadows, Giesecke's harebell stays extremely low and compact as an adaptation to fierce mountain winds.
Unlike the more common creeping bellflower which grows upright and has true bell-shaped flowers, trailing bellflower stays low to the ground with star-shaped blooms.

Common harebell is much more delicate and slender than its bellflower relatives like creeping bellflower or clustered bellflower, which tend to be more robust plants with upward-facing or clustered flowers.

Canterbury bells stand out among their bellflower relatives primarily due to their impressive size - both the individual flowers and overall plant are much larger than species like common harebell or creeping bellflower.
Giant Bellflower stands out from other New England bellflowers by its impressive size and distinctly broad, heart-shaped leaves.
Among New England's bellflowers, Cornish bellflower stands out with its fuzzy, grayish leaves and pure white hanging bells.
